title: Kioxia XL1 CXL XL-FLASH NAND Device Shown
gist: Kioxia showed a working XL1 at FMS 2026: a 512GB CXL 2.0 Type 3 memory-expansion device in E3.S form factor built on XL-FLASH Generation 2 NAND rather than DRAM, demonstrated at just under 1GB/s with 755ns latency and just shy of 2M IOPS on 100% 512B loads. The pitch is DRAM-shortage arbitrage - use cheap NAND for cold memory pages and DRAM for hot data - reviving the tiered-memory idea Intel Optane failed to commercialize, now delivered over a standard EDSFF slot that can alternatively hold an NVMe SSD.

insights.claim: DRAM is in such short supply that system designers are getting creative about sourcing memory capacity, and Kioxia is now offering a NAND-based CXL device so buyers can add memory capacity without paying the DRAM price per gigabyte.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: DRAM scarcity is now severe enough to pull substitute media into the memory tier - watch NAND suppliers as a second-order beneficiary of the memory shortage, not just DRAM makers.
insights.quote: These days, DRAM is in such short supply that folks are getting creative in providing memory capacity.

insights.claim: The economic case for the Kioxia XL1 is tiering: servers use NAND for colder memory regions while keeping DRAM for hot data, lowering total memory cost rather than beating DRAM on speed.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Adoption depends on workload hot/cold page distribution, so the addressable market is memory-capacity-bound workloads with skewed access patterns, not latency-critical ones.
insights.quote: XL1 lets servers use NAND for colder memory regions while using DRAM for hot data, lowering costs.

insights.claim: A DRAM-based CXL solution is undoubtedly faster than the XL1's NAND-based approach, so the product competes on cost per gigabyte rather than on performance parity.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Do not read this as NAND displacing DRAM in the memory tier; it is a capacity-per-dollar play that only clears if DRAM pricing stays elevated.
insights.quote: Undoubtedly, a DRAM-based CXL solution can be faster than the XL1’s NAND-based solution.

themes.theme: XL1 device specifications and measured performance

insights.claim: The Kioxia XL1 shown at FMS 2026 is a 512GB CXL 2.0 Type 3 device, meaning it is a memory expansion device rather than a coherent accelerator or cache attachment.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Type 3 memory expansion is the only CXL class with broad host support today, so this product avoids the ecosystem risk that stalled more ambitious CXL device types.
insights.quote: Since it is a Type 3 device, it is a memory expansion device.
insights.locator: Here is the little spec sheet that was at the show

insights.claim: A live Kioxia XL1 demonstration showed the 512GB device running at just under 1GB/s with 755ns latency, and just shy of 2M IOPS on a 100% 512B load.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Sub-microsecond latency at 755ns puts NAND-backed CXL roughly an order of magnitude above DRAM latency but far below SSD, defining exactly which tier of the memory hierarchy it can serve.
insights.quote: Here you can see the 512GB device running at just under 1GB/s with 755ns latency.
insights.locator: While there was a device on the floor

insights.claim: The XL1 is built on Kioxia XL-FLASH Generation 2, which unlike TLC and QLC NAND offers much higher write endurance and lower latency - the property that makes NAND viable as a memory-tier medium at all.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Only specialty low-latency NAND qualifies for memory expansion, so the volume opportunity accrues to vendors with SLC-class or XL-FLASH-style product lines, not commodity QLC.
insights.quote: The advantage of XL-FLASH is that, unlike TLC and QLC NAND, it has much higher write endurance and lower latency.
insights.locator: Here is the little spec sheet that was at the show

themes.theme: EDSFF slot fungibility as the deployment unlock

insights.claim: The XL1 uses an E3.S form factor whose EDSFF connection runs CXL instead of PCIe, so the same server chassis can be populated with either traditional NVMe SSDs or CXL memory devices.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Reusing the existing EDSFF bay means no new server SKU is required, removing the biggest historical barrier to memory-tier hardware adoption and letting operators rebalance storage versus memory per rack.
insights.quote: For system designers, this is a flexible solution since the same system can have traditional NVMe SSDs or CXL devices attached.
insights.locator: The drive at the show was an E3.S form factor

themes.theme: Tiered memory as a recycled architectural bet

insights.claim: The idea of mixing faster DRAM regions with slower media regions has been around for some time, with Intel Optane the famous prior example - Intel's original plan involved dedicated Optane channels, and CXL was part of that broader memory-architecture vision.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Tiered memory previously failed commercially on economics and software support; the variable that changed is DRAM pricing, so the thesis is a price-spread trade rather than a new technical capability.
insights.quote: Intel Optane was a famous example, with Intel’s original idea being to have dedicated Optane channels

insights.claim: CXL's ability to place different types of memory behind the controllers mirrors the promise IBM and companies like Microchip made with OMI, so the memory-media-agnostic interface concept predates CXL's current adoption wave.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Earlier media-agnostic memory interfaces failed to reach volume, so interface capability alone is not the adoption signal - watch hyperscaler design wins instead.
insights.quote: It is similar to how IBM and companies like Microchip had the same promise with OMI.
